School vs workplace

1. Why communicate at all?

blocks.caption:
Share your input, get credit
for your work, raise issues, provide feedback.

blocks.html:
Reason What it means
Share your input The company hired you for your knowledge and experience, not to sit like a doll. In meetings, they want your ideas — for example, why a new app is less popular than a competitor’s.
Get credit for your work If you improved something, people should know it was you. Later, when the company gives new responsibilities, they remember your work.
Raise issues If something is wrong in how the team works, or you face a special problem, you must speak up about it.
Provide feedback Your seniors give you feedback. You also give feedback — even on your own manager. This is called upward feedback (or upward appraisal), and it is confidential. If you lead a team, you give them feedback too.

2. Whom to communicate
to — and whom not to

blocks.html:
Lecture example — the broken chair at “Wheelderness” You join Wheelderness, the world leader in tyres. On day one, one wheel of your office chair is broken.

✗ Wrong: Email the CEO: “How can the world leader in tyres have a broken chair wheel?” This is rude and shows poor judgment.

✓ Right: Quietly ask your neighbour or the person who showed you your desk: “Whom should I report this to? Email, call, or a ticketing system?” Then use that process.

4. Length of
communication: be efficient

blocks.html: At work, there is a lot of communication. So your message must be efficient. You are not writing a story.
blocks.text: At work, there is a lot of communication. So your message must be efficient . You are not writing a story.

blocks.html:
✗ Don’t (long and wrong) ✓ Do (short and right)
“As we all know, education forms one of the pillars of success. I have been focussed on accumulating a good quality education… In addition, since I am also involved in an electric car project, this has required me to travel for a contest. The last date for the registration was in the middle of the contest and I missed it for no fault of mine. The institute needs to have a flexible policy… register me for the course now.” “I need to register for the course, but missed the last date due to an official activity at the same time. I request you to let me know the procedure for late registration.”

  • Preaching: “The institute needs a flexible policy” — as if you know better.
  • Blunt order: “Register me for the course now.”

5. Sending emails

blocks.html: Email is one of the main ways to communicate at work. Follow three rules.
blocks.text:
Email is one of the main ways to communicate at
work. Follow three rules.

Rule 1:
Carefully decide the list of recipients

blocks.html: Recipients are the people you send the email to.
blocks.text: Recipients are the people you send the email to.

blocks.html:
✗ Don’t ✓ Do
Send the message to every higher authority whose email ID you can find. Take the time to find the appropriate person, and send it only to them.
blocks.text:
✗ Don’t ✓ Do Send the message to every higher authority whose
email ID you can find. Take the time to find the appropriate person , and
send it only to them .

blocks.caption:
Wrong: send to everyone up to
the CEO. Right: find the one correct person.

blocks.html: Just because an email ID is easy to add does not mean it is correct to add it. Sending to everyone shows very poor judgment, and that impression sticks to you.

blocks.html: Lecture example — course registration problem A university has many wings: research, academics, hostel, food, maintenance and more. A course registration problem should go to the academic person who handles it — not to the hostel, not to the food team, and not straight to the director.

Rule 2:
Formal emails are not social media messages

blocks.html:
✗ Don’t ✓ Do
Use emojis and abbreviations freely Write complete sentences and convey ideas without scope for misunderstanding

Rule 3: Formal
emails need to be well structured

team you lead

blocks.html:

blocks.text:
Constraint 1:
Audience — seniority and purpose

blocks.html: Think about the audience’s background: business people, investment bankers, general public, your technical team, senior management, or school children?

  • Your audience invests time too. 50 people × half an hour = 25 hours of total time. Don’t waste it.

blocks.alt: Ways to connect with your audience
blocks.caption:
Repeat a summary,
separate facts from opinions, pause for decisions, use familiar
formats.

blocks.html: 1. Repeat a summary slide from your previous presentation. In a weekly or fortnightly team meeting, start with last time’s summary: “Two weeks ago we were here. Now let’s see what we did.” Everyone starts from the same point.

blocks.html: 2. Separate facts from opinions. - A fact is data — for example, results of a properly done vaccine test on 10,000 volunteers. - Comparing your vaccine with a competitor’s often includes your opinion. - Both are fine. Seniors often want your professional opinion. But tell them clearly which is fact and which is opinion. Then they know what is certain and where they are taking a chance.

blocks.html: Types of illustration: tables, graphs, photographs, drawings, schematics — and mixes of these on one slide.

blocks.caption:
Table for exact values,
graph for trends, photo for realism, drawing or schematic to control
complexity.

blocks.html:
Type Best for Watch out for
Table Showing exact values (e.g. 3.6, 2.1) Keep the same number of decimal places in every cell. Give units.
Graph Showing a trend (goes up, comes down, goes up again) — a table can never show this shape Label both axes with quantity and units, and add a caption. A graph cannot show exact values easily (39.3 and 1297).
Photograph Realism — size, shape, space. Example: a fuel cell and hydrogen tank fitted on a cycle. Works for every audience. You need permission to use it.
Drawing Ideas you cannot see in a photo — charges, properties, or two types of wind turbine (horizontal axis vs vertical axis) —
Schematic Showing layout of parts (e.g. an electric vehicle: motor, battery, electronics) while controlling complexity —
Composite Text + sample photo + equipment photo + graph on one slide, so seniors don’t lose track across slides —

sections.title: Writing a Report — Why It Matters and Why It Is Hard

Why are writing skills
important?

blocks.caption:
A written report gives you
credit, keeps a record, and shapes company decisions.

blocks.html: 1. Credit for your work. If you only tell people about your work, it spreads by word of mouth. Soon nobody remembers it was you. A document with your name on it gives you credit.

Why is formal writing
difficult?

blocks.html: 1. Personal background. - We come from different communities, regions (urban/rural) and countries. - Our native language may not be English. We think in our language and translate. In writing, we only have words. - A reader may read your report 15 days later, in another country. You can’t see their face or fix confusion. So your writing must be clear on its own.

What is the purpose of
formal writing?

blocks.caption:
Inform, persuade — and do both
efficiently.

blocks.html:
Purpose What it means
To inform readers Tell them what work was done — a survey, an analysis, missing data found in 25 sources, etc.
To persuade readers Help the organisation make a decision. “Based on my work, I suggest we go this way.” If your analysis is good, seniors will follow your advice — and be impressed.
To do the above efficiently This is what makes writing formal. Novels and newspapers don’t need to be efficient (newspapers even place ads between news). Formal writing must be.

Part What to write
Title Says what the document is about. Example: “Weather prediction using a smaller set of variables”.
